questions.q: What physics do both QuEra's and Pasqal's neutral-atom platforms build on?
options: Atoms held in optical tweezer arrays, entangled via Rydberg blockade
Ions held in electromagnetic traps and manipulated with lasers
Superconducting circuits cooled in a dilution refrigerator
Photons routed through silicon photonic integrated circuits
questions.explain: QuEra and Pasqal both build on optical-tweezer trapping and Rydberg-blockade entanglement -- the neutral-atom physics covered in the previous lesson, distinct from trapped-ion, superconducting, or photonic approaches.

questions.q: What is the difference between 'analog' and 'digital' modes on neutral-atom hardware?
options: Analog mode evolves the system continuously under a programmed Hamiltonian for tasks like optimization or simulation, while digital mode applies discrete gate sequences more like other gate-based platforms
Analog mode only works at cryogenic temperatures, while digital mode works at room temperature
Analog mode is used exclusively by Pasqal, and digital mode is used exclusively by QuEra
There is no real difference; the terms are interchangeable marketing language
questions.explain: Analog mode is continuous Hamiltonian evolution for problems like optimization/simulation, while digital mode uses discrete gates -- both companies pursue both modes, and the distinction is a real operational one, not interchangeable marketing.

questions.q: Why are neutral-atom systems genuinely able to report very large raw trapped-atom counts?
options: Because tweezers are generated optically rather than fabricated as individual physical structures, making it comparatively straightforward to project many tweezer sites and load atoms into them
Because neutral atoms never experience any loss once trapped
Because raw atom count is a meaningless number that companies can report however they like
Because neutral atoms require no lasers at all, simplifying the hardware
questions.explain: Since tweezers are projected optically rather than fabricated one at a time, scaling the raw number of trap sites and loaded atoms is comparatively easier than, say, fabricating and wiring an equivalent number of superconducting circuits -- a real structural advantage, not a fabricated claim.

questions.q: Which of the following is a real, open engineering challenge for neutral-atom platforms, even as raw atom counts grow large?
options: Gate fidelities lagging behind leading platforms, ongoing atom loss requiring active reloading, and risk during 2D/3D rearrangement of atoms for gates
Neutral atoms being too heavy to trap with any laser power available today
The complete absence of any cloud access to neutral-atom hardware
An inability to encode any qubit state in a neutral atom at all
questions.explain: Gate fidelity gaps, atom loss requiring reloading schemes, and the time/loss risk of physically rearranging atoms for 2D connectivity are the real engineering challenges that sit between a large raw atom count and a reliable, large-scale computation.

questions.q: Why does the lesson caution against treating 'largest qubit count' headlines as a scalability verdict on their own?
options: Because raw trapped-atom count is not the same as the number of high-fidelity, well-connected, error-corrected logical qubits actually usable for a computation
Because qubit counts reported by any company are always fabricated and should be ignored entirely
Because only superconducting platforms can ever have a meaningful qubit count
Because logical qubits and physical qubits are simply two different words for the exact same thing
questions.explain: A large number of loaded atoms doesn't by itself tell you about gate fidelity, atom loss rates, or connectivity -- the things that actually determine how close a system is to usable, error-corrected computation, which is why the two numbers must be kept distinct.
